LIES LAST HoURs.-Life's last hours
are grand testing hours. Death tries all
our principles, and lays bare all our foun-
dation. Vast numbers have been found to
act the hypocrite in life, who were forced to
be honest in the hour of death. What athe-
lists have owned their principles, what
worldlings have bewailed their folly when
death approached! Misgivings of the heart
that have been kept secret through life,
have come out in death and many who
seemed all right and fair for heaven, have
had to declare that they had only been self
deceived. 1t has been said, "man may not
dissemble in DEATH" hence the value of
dying testimonies. We gather the last acts,
the last experiences; and we treasure them
up as indubitable evidences in favor against
the character Of those that wore their value
as tests Of character, and all have felt their
force.

| What brave. glorious snow storm it
was, though! The boys built great
snow house, dipping the chunks of snow
in the water to harden them, so they
might last longer; and they rolled large
snow balls for a pyramid, till it was
higher than the school house. They
worked bravely, but the brightest face
and pleasantest voice among them was
Ben Bolts. Such rides as they had down
hill! and the larger boys and girls said
Alice May was too little and cowardly to
Din them, become she felt fearful some
times, yet Ben Bolt held her in his arms,
and away they went, merrily as any of
the rest. - ....
But the Winter began to wane, and
now and then soft, mild day would
come that lessened the pyramid and snow
house materially. ''Such a pity" they
said, and wished Winter would last al
ways; but there was one little, wren
like voice, that prayed for violets and
| blue birds. 81


The pyramid tumbled down, the snow
house grew thinner and thinner, and the
boys jested about its being in decline,
till one day it disappeared-faded away
like so many of their childish hopes.


The glad Spring came with its larks
and days, and one delightful day the
children went Maying. Kate Ashley
was queen, and a brilliant queen she was
too. bat Ben Bolt gathered white violets,
and braided them in the soft curls of
Alice, and told her she was sweeter.
dearer than thousand May queens like
Kate. Child as she was, his words made
the sun shine brighter, and lent enchant-
ment to the atmosphere. of her existence.


Then the long June days came, encir-
cling the green earth with a coronal Of
roses, and making it redolent with per-
| fume and in the warm noontide hour the
children strolled to the foot of the hill,
and clustering together, told over their
childish hopes of the future. Some were
| lured by ambition some dreamed of quiet
repose; some of gay city life; but there
was one whose eye kindled and young
face flushed with enthusiasm, as he spoke
of the sparkling blue waters, and the
brave ships that breasted them so gal
lantly.


Ben Bolt was going to sea. Captain
Shirley, a generous, whole-souled being
as ever trod the deck, was to take him
under his protection the next five years
| There was eXclamations of surprise and
sorrow from the children old haunts
were visited and revisited they sat down
in the shade Of the old sycamore, and lis
tened TO the musical murmur of the brook,
and the dreamy hum of "Appleton's
mill ;" exchanged keepsakes and promised
to remember the merry, brave-hearted
boy, whose home would be the wide blue
ocean.


Alice May seldom joined them. She
was so delicate and timid, and the thought
of Bens departure filled her eyes with
| tears, SO she would steal away alone,
| fearful of the ridicule of her harder COM
panionS.


But one night Ben came to Mr.. Mays
cottage, to bid them good-by. Alice
stood by the window watching the stars,
wondering what made them so dim-never
thinking Of the tears that dimmed her
eyes, as Ben told over his hopes so joy
fully. She could not part with him there,
so she walked through the little door
yard, and stood beside the gate, looking
like golden crowned angel in the yellow
moonlight; and when he told her over
again how large she would be on his re-
turn, that he would not dare to call her
| little Alice then; as he looked back lin
gerincly, she laid soft brown curl in his
hand, saying-s'I have kept it for you
this long, long time, Ben; ever since you
brought me home through the snow-do
| you remember -


He did remember. and with one passion
ate burst of grief, he pressed the little
| girl to his bosom, and the brave-hearted
| boy sobbed the farewell he could find no
words for,


But five years are not always life
time. True, it was such to the quiet,
thoughtful Charlie Allen, whose large,
dark eyes had stolen brilliancy from his
books; and the laughing little Bel Ar
cher-both were laid to sleep in the old
church yard, when the night-stars shone
on their graves. Others went out to seek
fortune in the gay world, and some grew
into miniature men and women by their
own sweet firesides; but Alice May seemed
still child. Yet she was taller, and her
slight form more gracefully developed;
but there was the same angel looking
through her eyes as had watched there

FIRST DECISION UNDER THE New STEAMBOAT
LAw.-The inspectors Of steamboats, at Cincinnati,
appointed under the new steamboat law passed by
Congress, have made thorough investigation into
all the facts touching the recent collision on the
Ohio Of the steamers Falls City and the Pittsburg
The testimony elected established the following
facts:-The night was foggy one when the collis
ion occurred and the rules and regulations requiring
the ringing Of the bells and blowing the whistle at
intervals OF two minutes, when running in the fog,
were not complied with. Had they been complied
with the collision would not have taken place As it
was, laudabe efforts were made by both boats, par.
ticularly the Falls City, to prevent it. The signal
bell of the Falls City was tapped twice, signify
ing her wish TO 60 to the lerboard, arid that
Of the Pittsburg tapped once, expressing desire to
60 the starboard but unfortunately the signal
one was not understood by the other. It was also
proven that the collision would have been rendered
less harmless had both boats instantly stopped on
discovering each other. This was done by the Falls
City, but not 80 promptly by the Pittsburg In view
OF all the facts, they acqut the two engineers who
were on duty at the time, and suspend for twenty
days the license of John White, the pilot Of the
Pittsburg, and the license Of jeremiah Mason, the
pilot Of the Falls River for ten days. for not observ-


ing the rules and regulations. The inspectors state
that the penalty in this case il made light from the
fact that the rules are new, and as yet mperfecty
understood but thatin oil future cases they shall
exact the most rigorous penalties Of the law.

LOUISVILLE, August ia returned
Californian, who had reached Independ-
ence, gives the following account of the
Indian battle, before reported, as having
occurred between the Sioux and Pawnee
Indians.


The Sioux were aided in the war by
the Cheyennes Indians. and the combined
forces were about 5000 strong. The
Pawnecs were assisted by the Iowas, Saxs
and Pottawattomies, numbering in all
about 5000. The opposing forces met
about fifty miles from Fort Kearney, and
the battle lasted all day, resulting in the
loss on both sides of from five to six
hundred killed. The Sioux party, though
the most numerous, were defeated


A person who has come in from Fort
Laramie, says the above account is exag-
gerated, but says that great demonstra-
ton was made, and had not the Pottawat-
omies interfered, the Pawnees would
have been defeated. He thinks that
hundreds, instead of thousands, would be
nearer the mark, as to the actual numbers
engaged, and the number killed was
doubtless much exaggerated.

The Exploring Expedition under Lieuten-
ant Lynch left the American flag floating
above the waters of the Dead Sea, secured
from all enemies but the wind. Lieuten-
ant Dale died soon after leaving the Dead
Seal


Wind Of the desert, sweeping on,
With pinion bold and free,
Oh, spare that flag which floats alone
Upon the silent sea
In that dread solitude unroll'd


To thy destructive breath,
And gaily shines each spang1ed fold,
When all around is death.
Darkly the rugged mountains frown
Upon the waves below,
Like pride and anger looking down
Upon O scene of woe.
The sluggish sea, the burning skies,
Speak only Of despair.
That tells that hope, and enterprise,
And courage have been there.
Brave hands unfurp that pennon free,
And dauntless hearts were near;
They left the flag of liberty


Above the waters drear,
And turn'd away, their task fulfll'd,
In other scenes to roam;
While even there each bosom thrill'd
With joyful thoughts of home.
But one, whose bright and fearless eye
First saw that banner wave,
Was doom'd beneath foreign sky
To find an early grave.
Deaths fatal shafts had found their way
Unto his manly breast;
Beneath the sunsets golden ray


They bore him to his rest.
In other days, when power divine


Watch'd Ger the Holy Land,
The sky would oft in brightness shine,
By angels pinions fann'd.
Now, though no angel parts the sky
With wings of waving gold,
The path to Heaven is still as nigh
AS once in days Of old.
Sleep on-the vengeful wind may rend
The pennon on the sea,
And wave and storm their fury blend,
But not to injure thee.
Brief tribute may the stranger give
TO one who rests alone,
But still thy memory shall live


In true hearts like thine own.

To know thy being and to feel thy life;
The hope of thee through many pang she nursed


And when amidst anguish like the parting strife
The babe was in her arms, the agony
Was all forgot for bliss of loving thee
Be gentle to thy mother: long she bore


Thine infant fretfulness and silly youth;
Nor rudely scorn the faithful voice that DER


Thy cradle prayed and taught thy lisping youth.
Yes, she is old; yet on thy manly brow
She looks, and claims thee as her child cen now.
Uphold thy mother: close to her warm heart


She carried, fed thee, lulled thee to thy rest;
Then taught thy tottering limbs their untried art,


Exulting in the fedgiing from her nest;
And now her steps are feeble, be her stay,
Whose strength was thine in thy most feeble day.
Cherish thy mother! brief perchance the time


May be that she will claim the care she gave;
Passed are her hopes of youth, her harvest prime


Ofjoy on earth; her friends are in the grave,
But for her children, she could lay her head
Gladly to rest among the precious dead.
Be tender with thy mother: words unkind


Or light neglect from thee would give pang
To that fair bosom, where thou art enshrined


In love unutterable, more than pang
Ofvenom'd serpent. Wound not her strong trust,
AS thou would'st hope for peace when she is dust.
0, mother mine! God grant ne'er forget

The unreasonable, unextinguishable debt


owe thy love; but find my sweet employ
Ever through thy remaining days to be
To thee as faithful as thou vert to me.

Star that love-first lamp in heaven
When the grey twilight, dim with sleep,
Lies in deep shadows-I have given
This hour to gaze on thee and weep
To weep, that Mary, young and holy,
Who once, with white hand locked in mine,
Sang thy sweet praise, lies still and lowly
Where thy pale clusters nightly shine
Tree, through whose boughs the moonlight dance.
Tracing faint pictures on the skies,
Thou hadst the last, jmpassioned glanccs,
OF gentle Mary's dying eyes;
How will watch thee, fragile willow,
Fragile as she, the sinless maid,
Whose dear head lies upon the pillow
So early smoothed beneath thy shade.
Flower that love, thy hues have faded;
So had the light in Mary's eye,
When, with soft tresses lightly braided.
She looked too beautiful to die;
Here, gentle rose, when they had laid her,
White-robed, amid funereal gloom,
Of thy fair sister-aowers, made her
wreath to carry to the tomb
Cold star, above her bosom shining,


And willow, guarding still her rest,
Bright flower, thy tendrils Ger her twining,
know not which she loved the best;
But each to me is dear and holy,


Each, soft and tender memories wake,
Each tell of Mary, sleeping lowly;


I'll love them all, for her sweet sake.

Can it be! can you look back into the
depths of those clear, blue eyes, that seek
yours in such confding innocent trust; can
you deck those dimpled limbs, " fsarfully
and wonderfully made?" can you watch
with him the first faint streak Of light, that
ushers in another hapy day? can yeu paint
out to him the gold and purple sunset glory ?
can you look upward with him to the shiu-
ing host? or place in bis eager hand the
field of flowers that bend their dewy eyes
with grateful thanks and never name "Our
Father!"


When at dead Of night you watch beside
his sick couch; when you hush your every
breath to listen to his panied means; when
every gust of wind makes your cheek grow
pale; when you turn with trembling hand
the healing drops; when every tick of the
clock seems beating against your heart,
when the little pallid face looks beseeching-
ly into yours, for the "help" you cannot
give; oh where can you turn the suppliant
eye, if you see not the " Great Physician ?"


When health slowly returns, when the eye
brightens, and the red colors lip and cheek;
when the vacant chair is again filled; when
loving arms in playful glee twine around
your neck comes there from that woman's
heart of thine no burst of grateful thanks
to Him who notes even the sparrow's
fall?


Suppose Death comes! You fold away
the little useless robes; you turn with q
filing eye from toys and books and paths
those little feet have trod; you feel ever the
shadowy clasp of little hand in yours;
you turn heart-sick from the happy mothers,
who number no missing lamb from their
Hocks; sunny ringlet, rosy cheek, or
piping voice, gives yourheart death pang.
You walk the busy street, and turn your
head involuntarily when a little strange
voice calls 'tMother!' Oh d! where can you
look for comfort, if you believe not that the
"Good Shepherd folds your lamb to His
loving breast?


There is perfdy at your household hearth!



There are broken vows, which you may not
breathe to human ear! There is treachery
repaid for trust! Childhood looks ON with
sad wonder. You must 60 backward and
cast the mantle of evasion over the moral
deformity. Whence shall strength come to
your slender shoulders to bear this heavy
cross! How silence the ready tempter's
voices Where shall all those warm affec-
tions be garnered up? Gf not in heaven.)


Oh! YOU have no anchor! no rudder or
compass! Your little bark is adrift, at the
mercy of every pitiless gale! The sea is
dark and fearful, the pillows mountains
high, the sky black with darkness, if you
turn from the Great Pilot!

Another bright and heaven-created day
made earth an Eden, and all things wor-
shippers. Rejoicing nature revelled in
the suns warm rays, and tuned its
hymns of thankfulness with every whis-
pering breeze, in every gently murmuring
brook and stream. The feathered song
sters fitted from tree to tree, from grove
to grove, and chirped with joyful glee
their notes of love and alteration. The
very f1ocks and herds lifted their meek
and patient eyes to heaven and offered up
their mute acknowledgements to Him who
having made, did not forget or fail to give
bountiful provision to meet his crea-
lures wants.


And while thus earth, and tree, and
flower, bird, beast, and natures SELF
raised one united paan to the author of
their being, where was the voice of man,
the last most perfect work of God! Did
human rapture louder swell the anthem,
did human hearts pour out the notes of
higher praise, to mount above and lead
the universal offering which rose to heav-
ems altar and mingled with the songs of
angels!


Alas. the curse is on us and is working
still. While all around, above, are striv-
ing which shall win approving smiles
from Deity, man, man alone, stands back
and riots in perverseness. Falsehood and
detraction labor to pull down the feeble
barriers which virtue raises, SANDER as
sails and blackens what it cannot initiate,
malice with fiendish hate pursues its VIC
tim to the very Threshold of eternity,
and Lucifer with grim, exulting smile,
looks ON to see the darkest of his foul
conceptions live, grow and flourish,
through the victims of his first deceit.

A MOTHERS AFFLrcr1oN.-A few days
ago pretty little boy, scarcely five years
old, while playing on some logs in the
Hamburg canal, suddenly slipped and
fell into the water. His little sister,
brave child ten years old, being near,
and seeing him sinking, flew to his as
sistance, and throwing herself fearlessly
into the canal, struggled to save her
perishing brother. Alas! two-fold fate
was therefor them. The poor boy sunk
for the last time, and his noble sister was
herself drowned in her fruitless efforts to
snatch him from watery grave. Who
dare repine at the minor miseries of daily
life, when they think upon the mother of
those drowned children, so dear to her?
No tears came as relief to her hot brain,
her constant cry was, "Give me my chill
drenm

line of friends followed the little victims
to their early grave, from their once
happy home at the Hydraulics. The
heart-worn mother still suffers the deep
agony of her bereavement, fit subject

Hath returned unto the skies;
Wipe the death-drops from her forehead
Sever one dear golden tress,
Fold her icy hands all meekly,

There-now softly say Good Night.

All life's trials to endure;

Round our necks so softly steal;
Our wet cheeks will miss the pressure

ent of the Placer (Caliiorn,a( Herald is

"A marriage took place on the nigh;
of the 18th ult., at the Nevada Hotel-a
lady not unknown to the California pub

party, their eyes met with mute express
i've establishment. The lady bride did

ened by the coincidence, and that his hap

in the history Of the United States that none Of the
great names among the American elected Presidents
had children. No one who was ever reelected has
had son. Washington had no children; he held
Office eight years. John Adams had children; he
was not reelected. jefferson had no children; he

had no children; held the Presidency eight years.

son died; Polk had no children; Taylor died; and
now, among the great names without children is the
next elected President after Taylor-President
Pierce, who, by an accident, is childless. The
event alone, added to his wellknown indifference to
holding power, will make him reelected like his
great chdless predecessors; and those who live will
see our prediction verified.

The Boston Herald states that young
married lady, living in Dover street. called
ut q store in Washington street some time
since. and made some purchases. After she
had paid for the articles, the senior partner
Of the firm asked her to step to the back
Of the store, where he accused her of steal
ing some articles, and in the most rude
manner proceeded to search her person,
but of course found nothing. The lady
upon reaching home was so shocked that she
was taken ill of fever, and remained sick for
three weeks. The storekeeper heard of this
.ickness, sent note apologising for his
rudeness, and requested permission to call
ut the house and further explain the matter
One day last week the lady sent word that
she would see him ON a certain evening.
The storekeeper called accordingly, aud was
shown into the back parlor. Soon after the
folding doors were thrown open, and the
husband Of the insulted lady led the as
tonished shopkeeper. forward into the bril-
liantly lighted room, where large party
was assembled, and introduced him as 1.-THE
gentleman who had accused his wife ofsteal-
ing After minute or two the gentle
nen of the house opened the door, when
one Of the young ladies present went TO the
piano and commenced the "Rogue's March"
The shopkeeper took the hint and left.

BosToN, Nov. 27.-Letters per steamer
Canada from Constantinople say that
another million of paper money had
been issued. IL was also stated that
Selim Pacha had crossed the Russian
frontier in Asia, and that news was
hourly expected Of a decisive battle hav.

decide the campaign.


The Russians have only 1000 fight

The general impression prevailed that
Russia would be defeated.


The Turks had taken by storm Cher
kedy, in Asia.


Advices from Rome state that the ex-
citing news from the banks of the Danube
has created some excitement among the
young soldiers of the French army of
occupation, and also among the oldest
veterans in the service, and that numer-
Gus applications have been transmitted
TO the competent authorities for permits
sion TO witness the operations of the
Turkish army.


The Dresden Journal contains some
details of the military preparations Of
Russia. Besides the three corps in the
Danubian Principalities and Bessarabia,
there is fourth movable corps in Volpy-
MIA and Podelia, and large masses Of
troops are concentrated in other places.
AT Krementshuck are eight regiments of
cuirassiers and four regiments of lancers,
and eight regiments of dragons are sta.
toned at Charkoco. Besides these, there
are numerous corps of Cossacks ready to
take the field. Large bodies of troops,
too, are marching to reinforce the army
under Prince Worouzoff.

Yesterday morning violent shower visited oul

the side Of the HILL and the crops in the
try. The rain poured down in torrents, and the

An ivymantled cottage smiled,


Deep-wooded near a streamlets side,
Where dwelt the village pastors child,


In all her maiden bloom and pride.
Proud suitors paid their court and duty
To this romantic sylvan beauty:
Yet nore of all the swains who sought her.
Was worthy of the pastors daughter.
The town gallants crossed hill and plain,


To seek the groves of her retreat,
And many followed in her train,


To lay the riches at her feet.
But still, for all their arts so soary,
From home they could not lure the fairy,
maid without heart they thought her,
And SO they left the pastors daughter.
One balmy eve in dewy spring,


A bard became her fathers guest:
He struck his harp, and every string


TO love vibrated in her breast
With that true faith which cannot falter,
Her hand was given at the altar,
And faithful was the heart he brought her
To wedlock and the pastors daughter.
How seldom learn the worldly CAV,


With all their sopbistry and art,
The sweet and gentle primrose-way


To woman's fond, devoted heart:
They seek, but never find, the treasure,
Although revealed in jet and azure;
To them, like truth in wells of water,
A fable is the pastors daughter.

BY THOMAS MOORE.
TO those we love We pledged tonight;
But now attend, and stare not,
While the ampler list recite


OF those for whom we care not.
For royal men, howeer they frown,
If on their fronts they bear not
That noblest gem that decks crown,
The peoples love-we care not.
For slavish men, who bend beneath
despot yoke, yet dare not
Pronounce the will, whose very breath
Would rend its links-we care not.
For priestly men, who covet sway
And wealth, though they declare not;
Who point, like finger posts, the way
They never go-we care not.
For martial men, who on their sword,
Howe'er it conquers, wears not
The pledges of soldiers word,


Redeemed and pure-we care not.
For legal men, who plead for wrong,
And, though to lies they swear not,
Are hardly better than the throrg
Of those who dove care not.
For courtly men, who feed upon


The land, like grubs, and spare not
The small leaf, where they can sun
Their crawling limbs-we care not.
For wealthy men, who keep their mines
In darkness hid, and share not
The paltry ore with him who pines
In honest want-we care not.
For prudent men, who hold the power
Oflove aloof, and bare not
Their hearts in any guardless hour
To beauty's shaft-we care not.
For all, in short, on land or sea,


In camp or court, who are not,
Who never acre, or e'er acM be


Good men and true-we care not.
